text: — Don’t rattle on too much, I’m telling you that we must choose government men! — cried Bay Ganyo and struck the table hard.
— But how are we going to elect government officials, where are we going to dig up voters from? Why, you, Bay Ganyo, aren’t you one yourself; supposedly a liberal — Bochoolu dared to object.
— Who told you that I am a liberal! — asked Bay Ganyo sternly.

— Who told me? Well, don’t you remember how many conservatives you thrashed, how much you cursed them—how could you not be a liberal? Don’t you know—you yourself said so—that you even boasted to Irechek that you were a liberal? — Bochooğlu objected.

— Hey, how stupid you are! — answers Bay Ganyo with a condescending smile. — So what if I told it to Yirechek, does a word make a hole? Come on, fool, if I don’t throw one at Yirechek, whom am I going to throw one at?
— You’re right, your grace! Bochoolu, lie low and keep quiet, don’t sing his funeral praises! — Gochoolu chimed in. — I’m a conservative too.

— Well, am I a tombstone or what! I’m downright a conservative too — blurted Dochoolu, — you get up too, Bochoolu, and become a conservative, so that we can grab those fellows and make sure they can’t move.
— Well, but I don’t know who the manager will be with — replies Bochoolu.

— The governor? He’s with us, of course — Bay Ganyo announces. — The district chief is with us too. The permanent commission isn’t legal, but who’s going to bother about legality? It’s ours. The bureau is ours. The city council is ours. The mayor is a little restless, but we’ll cut off his tail. The municipal councils in the villages haven’t been confirmed on purpose, do you understand? If they’re with us, we’ll confirm them; if not, to hell with them. I’m telling you again — as for the governor, don’t worry, he’s ours.
— And the porters? — Bochoo asks curiously.
— The porters are ours too, and the Gypsies, and Danko the Rogue is ours as well...
— But wasn’t he imprisoned for theft? — Bochoolu wonders.

— Eh-heh, you’re grazing ducks. We let him go ourselves. Didn’t he win us the porters? He went to them the other day, gathered them together, and when he snapped at them, they froze in their places, as he growled at them: “I’ll smash your teeth if you don’t elect Bay Ganyo!” — and the porters gave in. Danko bargained for them at two leva per man, and in return for the election, a whole night of food and drink.
— What a fearsome bandit, hey!

— And how much do you think! For 50 leva. He went to those people to ask for 100 leva, they drove him away, scolded him. You’ll see him now on Sunday — he’ll crush their bones! — says Bay Ganyo smugly.
— Bochoolu, go and call Gunya Advokatina to come here and write us an appeal, tell him: “Bay Ganyo is calling you.”

As soon as Bochoo left, Bay Ganyo lowered his head and, in a mysterious voice, turned to his companions:

— Keep quiet! We’ll keep fooling this brute right up to election day, telling him we’re going to make him a deputy. We’ll write just enough ballots with his name to make a show of it, and the other ballots will be written by the clerks in the Town Council and from the District Administration. Now listen to me: the minister wants me to be a deputy no matter what. You, Gochoolu, do you want to be?
— Well, I’d like to, Bay Ganyo — replies Gochoolu.
— I’d like that too — Dochoolu chimes in.

— Well, you’d like that, wouldn’t you, but, to tell you the truth, you’ve completely disgraced yourself in front of people. Why did you have to make yourself so visible; who was shouting in the squares: “Long live the great patriot!”, “Down with the vile tyrant!”, “To the gallows with Klimenta”, “Long live Kliment!”;
— Well, weren’t we all together, Bay Ganyo, why are you twisting the truth?

— Together, but our going out is all hush-hush. At last, well then, since you want it so much — all right, I’ll choose you. The fact that the peasants hate you and that you sold them their rugs because of your damned vanity...
— As for that, don’t talk, Bay Ganyo, for I know what sort of goods you are too — says Dochoolu cautiously.

Bay Ganyo is ready to boil over, but at that moment Gunyo the Lawyer comes in. Bay Ganyo tells him what the proclamation should be like. Gunyo sits down at the table, takes the pen, and sinks into thought. At Bay Ganyo’s order, the servant brings a bottle of mastika. Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Bay Ganyo drink, Gunyo writes. After half an hour, the following is ready:
APPEAL TO THE VOTERS OF OUR DISTRICT

In view of the great importance and significance which the forthcoming elections for народни representatives have for the present and future of our fatherland, our citizens, numbering more than 700 persons, gathered today in the yard of the school in Parcal mahlesi, and after discussing the matter of the candidacies of the persons for representatives, we remained in agreement and unanimously decided to recommend to the gentlemen voters of our district for народни representatives our fellow citizens:
Ganyo Balkanski, merchant, known throughout all of Bulgaria.
Philyu Gochoolu, a merchant with capital.
Tanas Dochoolu, merchant in the wine industry.
It was precisely those same persons whom the committee of the Народната партия had also recommended to you in its appeal of August 27 of last month.

By announcing this unanimous decision of ours to the other gentlemen electors from the town and our district, who have at heart the welfare of the Fatherland, the material improvement of the farmer, the easing of the taxpayer’s condition, in a word, the interests of our district, we invite them to vote in the election on the 11th of this month for the above-mentioned three fellow citizens of ours, in whom we have full confidence that they will worthily represent our region in the National Assembly.
Dear Voters,

You have already been presented by several citizens with a list containing the names of Nikola Tarnovaliyata, Lulcho Doktorov, and Ivanitsa Gramatikov, persons not from Our circle, persons foreign to Us, who do not have and cannot have Our trust. Perhaps others will also appear who will try to persuade you to vote for their candidates. We advise you, gentlemen voters, not to be deceived by their fine words, and not to yield to their flattery, and not to believe various rumors and fabrications spread by them about some district telegrams and the like. Nikola Tarnovaliyata is originally from the town of Tarnovo and therefore, out of spite for the flea, he burns the quilt. Lulcho Doktorov is entirely from the Trans-Danubian Province, and Ivanitsa Gramatikov is known to no one and, nota bene, he is a Russian-educated man, therefore a traitor to our dear Fatherland.
Dear voters,
We are convinced that the above-mentioned persons, that is, the following:
Ganyu Balkanski,
Philyu Gochoolu,
Tanas Dochoolu,

those who have complete devotion and kneeling loyalty to THE THRONE AND THE DYNASTY OF HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS OUR BELOVED PRINCE FERDINAND I, and who will faithfully support our present patriotic government headed by the current president-minister, will win your trust.
— Bravo, Ganyo — cried Bay Ganyo, — you turned out to be a whole Bismarck.
— Do you think I’m stupid? — Ganyo says smugly.
— Now go and take this to the print shop so they can print it in big letters, like this!
— Well, what about the money?

— There’s no money; tell him to print it like that, and if not, tell him that we’ll say to the City Council and the other offices not to have their papers printed with him. Do you understand? Come on now — commands Bay Ganyo.
— Do you know — continues Bay Ganyo — those who sent a telegram to the minister to complain that the governor had gone around the villages to agitate.
— Savages! — Gochoolu calls out.
— But what! — adds Dochoolu.
— The minister’s wife is not the Holy Virgin, to listen to them like that! He replied to them: the elections are free, ha-ha-ha!...
— Ha-ha-ha! — giggle Gochoolu and Dochoolu.

— Terrible devil, damn him. Freedom, is it? Freedom, indeed! They’ll see what freedom is on Sunday, and they’ll remember it for life. Especially Gramatikov! The poor man hasn’t seen our elections yet. Let those fellows of ours, those Gypsies with bloodshot eyes, with two fingers sticking out, those hoarse throats, those belts up to the neck, come out to meet him; let them stare him down, and then let that boar, Danko Harsuzina, come up behind him and just shout: “Hold him!”
— Ha-ha-ha! — Gochoolu and Dochoolu giggle, their eyes shining with delight.

— Li-be-ra-ls! Con-sti-tu-tion! Nn-a, consti-tution! They’re always hoping for the “circular telegram.” They’ve deafened people’s ears with this circular telegram. They’re always reading it, always pointing to it in front of everyone. We were laughing yesterday with the governor in the café. Just for appearances, he had that blasted telegram printed and sent around to the cafés. Yesterday we’re sitting with him in the café, watching those ones, with their heads bent over a table, like sheep at noon, reading, reading the telegram, rejoicing, we hear them whispering: “Free! The elections are free! The police won’t interfere!” And the governor and I were he-he-he! I glance at him out of the corner of my eye and say jokingly: “We’re sure!” He bursts out laughing and hop — a mastika. He pats his pocket — meaning that letter about the freedom of the elections, winks and says: “We’re not sure,” and he-he-he! Hop! Another mastika... We got thoroughly plastered!... Then Dancho the Rascal came too, and others, and others, and when we shut ourselves up in the café, when I shouted to the fiddlers: now then! They snapped their strings!... Georgy’s mastika isn’t any good, and the meze is lousy too; instead of making pickles, he serves sour okra!... Ugh! My head’s been aching since yesterday. Gochoolu, pour me another mastika.
— For a hangover!
— Never mind that, we have to drink again tonight. From this evening we must arrange the men in the taverns.
— Isn’t it too early, Bay Ganyo? — Dochoolu chimed in.

— It’s not too early; tomorrow is Saturday, there are still 36 hours left to drink. It’s not too early! Just right! And at last there won’t be the same ones always drinking. They’ll take turns. Some will drink for 5–6 hours, then rest, and others will start. In order, in order! Once they get together, they won’t be going home. They’ll drink there, eat there, sleep there! Do you understand?
— We know, is this the first time we’re holding elections! — Gochoolu chimed in.

— You, Gochoolu, when you pass by Arnautina’s place, tell him to get 300 okas of bread ready for this evening and send them — 100 okas to the Gypsy quarter at Topachoolu’s, 100 okas to Parcal mahlesi at Gogov’s tavern, and 100 okas down below, to the porters. You, Dochoolu, go by these taverns and tell them to start giving wine and rakia from this evening. More rakia, let them give them, did you hear? And tell them not to overcharge too much, or the devil will take them. Last year, for nothing at all, they fleeced us of 2,000 leva, the scoundrels! Tell them to use their heads, because the City Council is ours! Go also past the butchers and tell them, whatever offal, liver, intestines, bones they have, let them gather it into one or two baskets, because we’ll send it to the taverns so they can boil a pot of soup for our people. Tonight the governor and the district chief will return from the villages; I’ll take them with me to go around the other taverns and cafés. We’ll gather people from all the offices to write ballots; we’ll make them write all night. I’ve chosen the paper, that grayish, yellowish kind. We’ll fold our ballots like amulets...
— Yuch-kyushelii — explains Dochoolu.

— Yuch-kyushelii. But we need to get hold of a few of their ballots, to see what kind of paper they use and how they fold them, so that I can have the scribes write 1,000–2,000 ballots on their paper with our names.
— You’re a terrible devil, Bay Ganyo, you’ve learned those things inside out! — says Gochoolu with reverence.

— Fine work! Why am I Ganyo Balkanski if I’m not going to know this trade too? You, sir, put me in whatever district you like and tell me whoever you want me to elect. Put a donkey up as a candidate, and I’ll elect the donkey, by God! Just give me the district chief with the gendarmes and give me 1,000—2,000 leva. Let me gather for you, my friend, those sons of bitches of mine from the stake, from the noose, some 40—50 thugs, and line them up in two or three taverns on the outskirts, put a bucket over each of their heads, and then shout to them: “Hup bakalam! Long live Bulgaria!” Heh-heh! Are you there, Penka!... When those bulging eyes of mine turn bloodshot, when they start pulling those knives of theirs from their belts and stabbing them into the tables, when they raise such a racket with those hoarse, rasping voices of theirs — it’ll scare the living daylights out of you! Then take them and lead this horror through the middle of town at night... Opposition, is it?... The devil himself couldn’t stand up to you! Take them past the house of some opponent... My goodness! When they open those throats of theirs!... If you hear them from a mile away, ants will crawl under your skin, and your hair will stand on end like a hedgehog’s!... Then summon the village mayors and clerks, flash your eyes at them, grind your teeth at them, and point out those sons of bitches... Voters, are they?... — You won’t even see their shadow! When 12 municipal councilors from each village, along with the mayors, come flocking to you, when you gather the officials and clerks, place gendarmes at the edges to turn back the other peasants, surround the office with those 40—50 ruffians, make some kind of racket, stuff a few bundles of ballots into the boxes, and there you have your donkey as a народен представител, ha-ha-ha!
— Ha-ha-ha — responded Gochoolu and Dochoolu, — bravo, Bay Ganyo!
— Yes, but the police alone aren’t enough; the office has to be yours too — Gochoolu adds.
— I think so too — Dochoolu chimed in. — It’s ours now, but I’m saying, you know... Really, Bay Ganyo, do tell me, please, how did you manage to get that bureau?

— How so? — replies Bay Ganyo with a self-satisfied smile. — Very simple! Didn’t we elect a district council? Eight of theirs were elected, four of ours. We got the four of theirs annulled, the more important ones... But you’ll say there was an uproar. To hell with it! By the time they sort it out — the elections will be over. That left four of theirs and four of ours. But from theirs we left only the poor ones. We gathered to elect a standing committee. The messenger couldn’t find one of theirs — do you see?
— T... t... t...! — clicks Dochoolu. — What Bismarck! Bismarck can’t even turn your slippers over!

— Wait, what do you mean, what else have you seen? After all, are only the Germans the ones who have a Bismarck?... Anyway: we stayed, effendi, three of theirs, four of ours, majority! Well, of course, we don’t have yellow on the beak — the commission turned out entirely ours. Leave that aside, but more votes were received for our people, because to two of theirs we had separately promised that we would elect them as associate secretaries, and they, the fools, vote and vote for our people... ha-ha-ha! Now they walk the streets like opium smokers. Especially one of them, an influential gentleman, we took him with us in the villages to agitate, having promised to elect him secretary, and he, the savage, went and left his job... He abandoned the tame one to chase the wild one. Fool!... Dochoolu, pour me another mastika.
Bay Ganyo strained the mastika through his mustache, wiped himself with the palm of his hand, twirled “those damned things,” and continued:

— Now let me tell you how a bureau for the elections is chosen. It is done by lot. The chairman of the court draws it. That is called “by lot,” but I can choose whomever I want for you. And very easily: if you put the ballots in a glass, so they can be seen from outside, you should draw a line with ink on each of the filled ballots; and if they are in a box, you should take a deeper box, so the ballots cannot be seen from the side, and you will arrange the filled ones on one side and the empty ones on the other. After that, all that remains is to whisper to the chairman that “his business is busted” and therefore “he should keep his eyes open”... They call out: Ivan, Stoyan, Pŭrvan! Do you need Pŭrvan? — take a filled ballot. Don’t you need Pŭrvan? — take an empty ballot. In other words, the chairman draws the lot...
— Damn that Bay Ganyo! And those boors found someone to fight with. Pity them — said Gochoolu.
— And with that head, you still haven’t become a minister! — Dochoolu wonders.
— Well, shut it! — says Bay Ganyo modestly. — You know the Bulgarians!...

At dawn, the east is barely beginning to brighten, and a pale light is spreading through the interior of Gogov’s tavern in Partzal mahlesi. Around thirty sturdy fellows are sprawled across the tables, on the floor, on chairs; snoring, as though thirty tigers were locked in struggle, is heard from the street and disturbs the hearing of the police watchman. From time to time one of these fellows raises himself with half-closed eyes, steps over the corpses, gropes with his hands for the jug, and greedily quenches the alcoholic fire that sears his stomach, throat, mouth, and cracked lips; the dead men trampled by him in the dungeon awaken and pour out curses and oaths with hoarse, dried-up throats. Stench! A hellish stench their breaths give off, poisoning the already poisoned air in the tavern, saturated by the vapors of this mass of gloomy heroes.

Gochoolu and Dochoolu are already awake and drinking coffee in Keles Hasan’s café. It is already time for the sleeping camps of the electoral army to wake up. Here they are now in front of Gogo’s tavern. They open the doors, and a wave of stifling stench drives them back.
— Phew! May the devil take them! — cries Gochoolu in a choked voice and pinches his nose.
— Did they eat garlic, who knows! — Dochoolu says through clenched teeth with a sour grimace and also pinches his nose.
Through the open door, fresh air rushes into the tavern and gives the not-so-sensitive pair the opportunity to get inside.
— Are you still sleeping, you cattle? Get up at once! — commands Gochoolu authoritatively and starts kicking the drunken squad with his feet.
— Gogo, give them each a shot of rakia so they can open their eyes — adds Dochoolu.

Gogo lazily gets out of his bed, stretches, yawns, scratches himself in the sweaty places, and reluctantly starts rummaging among the bottles and glasses. The rakia, poured, he offers to the soundly sleeping lads.
— Get up, donkey, come on, eat! Stop yawning like a dog. Look at your eyes — bulging like boils! Come on, swallow!

With such courtesies, aided also by energetic kicks, Gogo goes around the guests, stiffened by drunkenness, and offers them rakia to bring them to their senses. Here and there someone will growl in protest at Gogo’s kicks, another will glare back at him with fierce, bloodshot eyes, and someone may even make an attempt to spring up and seize the handle of the fisherman’s knife stuck in his belt. These terrifying movements fill the souls of Gochoolu and Dochoolu with delight. They whisper to each other:
— Down there, look at that big fellow over there, in the corner, with the bandaged eye, do you know him?

— How could I not know him — Petrescu, the one who drowned his father in the swamp! I know him! God forbid you should fall into his clutches! Do you see what kind of knife he has tucked in there! And do you know that one over there, under the counter?
— That fat guy, the one bandaging the wound on his leg?
— No, the other one, with the torn lips.
— I can’t think of it... Ha, wait, wasn’t it that bastard of Sersem Petsa who robbed the church?

— No. Sersam Pecinoto is that one over there, lying next to the hajduk Boncho, and this one is Danko Harsuzin’s grandson. Bay Ganyo sent him here to keep an eye on these idlers so that the others might not lure them away. A terrible hajduk indeed! Didn’t he steal that evening a bundle of their ballots.
— Bravo!

— Do you know what we assigned him for? When we rush around the desk, if theirs should come, this kid will grab Nikola Tŭrnovaliya by the collar and start shouting: “Hold him! This one is cursing the prince! The prince is being sworn at, hold him!” Then Petresku and Danko Harsŭzina will seize Nikola and throw him out. The police will take him and — into the lockup. Theirs will want to get him out, and we — against them. There will be a clash. The police will burst in and scatter them like chicks. It’s arranged.
— Well, who’s going to touch Lulcha and Gramatikova?
— Do you take them for people? If a Topachoğlu were to glare at them head-on, they’d lose their heads.

Such a conversation is being held by Gochoolu and Dochoolu as they watch with delight the sluggish awakening of those thirty dark figures, gathered from the stake and the rope, who today are tasked with frightening, driving away, spreading terror and dread around the polling place, and making the already frightened Bulgarian renounce his barely conscious right to exercise his free will in the governance of the state. Such a conversation is being held by Gochoolu and Dochoolu as they look at those thirty terrible figures, disfigured, swollen, with bulging bloodshot eyes, wounded, scratched, with wide sashes, with knives at their belts, with ferocity on their faces, with criminal convulsions in their movements; they look at them and anticipate the sweetness of electoral victory.

All the mercenaries were already on their feet when music was heard from the Gypsy quarter... Music! Shall I describe this music, which had spent the whole night performing in Topachoolu’s tavern, in front of which the tavern-keeper himself had been wriggling and singing: “Vangelito chuvre shilo, na chuvreto sagreshilo, ya grumni, bozhé, udari me i po-skoro priberi me.” Shall I describe the fiddler, asleep on his feet, with the violin lazily resting almost on his belly? Shall I tell you about the clarinetist, who either does not play at all, or else, like a madman, will blow the clarinet, puff out his face, the veins in his neck will bulge, his bloodshot eyes will bulge, and it seems to you that with just a little more effort, a terrible epileptic fit will astound the listeners? No, I will not describe the music, because I think it is enough to tell you only that these musicians were à la Bay Ganyo.

The music was playing the Pecheneg March... Amid the interrupted sounds, a wild, a mixed roar split the air. A whole cloud of birds fearfully left the trees and the eaves of Parcal mahala. If an army of hungry lions were to face an army of enraged tigers, and at a signal those armies were to hurl themselves one against the other, the roar that would shatter the battlefield would be like the wild roar that now frightened the inhabitants of the Gypsy quarter and Parcal mahala. It was a “hurrah” from the mercenaries gathered by Danko Harsazina. There they are, appearing from around the bend in the street and pouring into the square.

The music in front, behind the music the gypsies and porters. At the head, lifted on hands, with twisted mustaches, with a tilted hat... who do you think? — None other than our own Bay Ganyo Balkanski. Even at this solemn moment Bay Ganyo does not forget himself: he keeps his hands in his pockets: “Heaven help us, some bandit might reach in — and the purse is gone. I know my goods.” A second “hurrah,” enough to wake even the dead, deafened the ears of Gogov’s crowd, which spilled out of the tavern onto the square and answered with a cannonade: “Long live Bay Ganyo!”
— Good morning, boys — called out the beaming Bay Ganyo condescendingly.
A mishmash of thirty hoarse “good mornings” answered his greeting.

— Courage, boys, the strength is with us — encourages Bay Ganyo in the tone of Napoleon before Austerlitz. — Listen, you, Danko’s grandchild, do you remember what I told you: when you see trouble, grab Tŭrnovaliyata by the collar, and shout: “The prince is cursing.” Did you understand?
— I know — Dancho’s grandson calls out cheerfully from the ranks. — And you, Danko, and you, Petrescu...
— We know... upside down — said Petrescu, fully aware of the importance of his task.

— Bravo! Well, listen, Petrescu, I want one more trick from you: when you get into a fight with the voters, you stab only two or three of them with the knife, just enough to stun them, then throw the knife aside, then tear your shirt on the chest, then scratch your skin until it bleeds, do you understand? Then smear your face with blood, do you understand? Then after that start shouting that the citizens wanted to slaughter you because you shouted: “Long live the prince,” do you understand?
— I understand, but you’ll give me another five leva for the can-paras.
— For money — easy, you just do what I tell you — calms Uncle Ganyo.

The scouts sent on reconnaissance from the gypsy quarter toward the polling place, Adamcho Kokosharina, Spiro Kopoya, and Topal Mustafa, arrived hurriedly at the square and reported to Bay Ganyo that about three thousand peasants had arrived in the town by various roads and that the people of Tarnovaliya had distributed ballots to them. “The district officer said to hurry, because the business is blown.”

— Damn your district chief! — shouted Bay Ganyo. — What the hell did we appoint him chief for, if he can’t even rough up a few peasants? Chief! Cucumbers! He only knows how to flirt with the peasant girls. Fool! Why hasn’t he sent gendarmes to the outskirts? The donkey has stuffed himself so much he’s forgotten what he’s supposed to do. Run quickly and tell him to gather the mounted gendarmes and send them galloping through the middle of town, do you understand? Through the middle of town, like a storm, flying by, hear? And we’ll shout a big “hurrah” from here, so let’s see which peasant will dare stand up to us. Run quickly!

— Gogo, give me the rakia here — commands Bay Ganyo. — Eat up, damn it, I’m paying. Why are the fiddlers silent? Chalnuz, damn it, chengeneler! Blow the clarinet, man, why are you staring at me like a cow? Huh, that’s it! I-i-ih-ha-ha!
— Danko, hand out one bundle of ballots to everyone now! Come on now, boys, forward. Courage! Long live His Royal Highness, hurrah!...
— Hooray!...
And they set off... the voters!

Ivanitsa Gramatikov, the opposition candidate, woke up at six in the morning. He got dressed, drank his coffee, and went out onto the high veranda in front of the house. The sun, just risen, was reflected in the church dome and in the windows facing east. The whole of nature seemed triumphant. In fact, nature remained just as indifferent as it always is, and triumphant was only the candidate’s soul.

Young, educated, a little idealistic, more of a dreamer, with love in his heart, with faith in goodness, with hope for the future, he was not yet hardened by reality, by life. Carefree to the point of self-forgetfulness, an incorrigible optimist, accustomed to looking at everything from its good side, he was trusting to the point of naivety, to the point of foolishness.

Several friends proposed his candidacy for народен representative; an assembly of citizens sympathetically accepted this candidacy, and Gramatikov thought that everything was already over, and he floated away into dreams of the forthcoming activity in the National Assembly. Honey and butter flowed through Bulgaria. But some other details, some preparatory actions of his friends preceding the election, actions unforeseen in the electoral law, seemed now and then to cast a shadow over his sweet dreams. Why did he now have to present his program to the voters, as if it could not be done without that? Why did he have to endure so many awkward moments, to answer, to promise assistance for the satisfaction of needs that perhaps concerned only the questioners? It was as if he had entrusted his entire intellect to the surrounding staff of friends! They told him that he had to make a speech, and he made a speech. They told him that he had to receive the village mayors and speak to them kindly, and he received the mayors and clerks in his house and spoke to them so kindly that the peasants lowered their eyes and could hardly understand him. They stated their needs, he took notes, and honestly said what could be satisfied and what could not, to the peasants’ extreme displeasure, for they were used to being promised golden mountains. He had to take part in the meetings of the prominent citizens, at which the agitators for the villages and the city quarters were determined and assigned. The citizens argue, make noise, and he sits aside and is silent, as if this did not concern him. This foolish passivity worries him; he opens his mouth to say something, to object, but someone from the staff will seize him by the hand and say to him in a fatherly, patronizing tone: “You keep quiet, stay aside, you still do not understand these things.” And he would obediently fall silent and listen to the solid and self-assured conversations of the respectable citizens. “Do elections always happen like this,” he thinks, “or is this perhaps beginning now, with the new era?” He nudges one of the disputants and whispers in his ear: “Please tell me, do elections always happen like this?” The disputant, absorbed in another conversation, looks at him as through a mist and says with a smile, in a didactic tone: “Leave that for another time; you don’t understand these things, stay aside: everything is in order.”

The work is all right! Gramatikov got used to the thought that the work was all right. Wherever he sat, wherever he stood, with whomever he met—merchant, craftsman, peasant—he kept hearing the same thing: that the work was all right. If he went to the café, friends would gather around him and hurry to bring him news from the town and the villages: “Oh, good morning, Mr. Ivanitsa, how are you? Well, now the work is all right.” “Oh, Mr. Ivanitsa, it was! I could pull the whole district out of my pocket. Enjoy yourself! The work is now completely all right!” If he went for an evening walk in the town garden, friends would meet him along all the alleys and from afar make signs to him with their hands—that is to say, it was so, the work was all right...

All right! But one incident, which he witnessed on the eve of the elections, made him understand that there is a difference between the elections as outlined in the electoral law and the elections in reality. This incident was recalled to him in a letter by a friend of his in the following words: “Legality, order, freedom, our success... Do you remember, do you remember? — Jumbush! Do you remember the invasion of the Huns in the café on the evening before the elections. Do you remember that ‘Bulgarian citizen’ with the Russian cap on the back of his head, bare-chested, barefoot, with torn knees? And what about that one with the red eyes, in his shirt, bareheaded, with the big club in his hand? And what about the Vlach outside by the door, who in the valiant ‘intoxication’ of patriotism, in the deep awareness of his free civic rights and duties, ripe, that is, already ripened in political wisdom, could barely stand on his feet? Do you remember how, with chests swollen by the noblest and most humane ideas, worthy of making an entire world happy, with a tongue thickened by the effort of the inexpressible and sublime thoughts that stirred his brain, do you remember how he declaimed about freedom and народни rights, so that when an older citizen, coming out of the café, shouted at him, freedom and народни rights stuck in his throat, just as they had stuck somewhere in the noble soul of his moral fellow partisan and chief? And this mob, this sediment from the mud of a wild, bestial civic stratum, devoid of all education and upbringing, ready for any brutality, which I could not even imagine existed in our city, so self-satisfied with its own ‘civilization’ and ‘Europeanism,’ this unprincipled crowd, led by its various ignoramuses and men without character, who have no principles and cannot have any; and this mob, I say, has its representatives in the National Assembly, while the thousands of voters...”

And so, on Sunday, on election day, around seven o’clock in the morning, Gramatikov was standing on the high veranda of the house and, with ease and joy, was taking in the morning coolness. The electoral law, enlivened in his dreams, was sequentially painting for him the various moments of a constitutional election. The city clock, announcing the half hour with two strikes of the bell, interrupted the candidate’s sweet dreams and reminded him that it was time to set off for the polling place. He dressed, took his little cane, but remembered that it was forbidden to enter the election with any kind of weapon, left his cane behind, and set off... The streets were almost empty; the people had already drifted down toward the schoolyard. In the square in front of the church, a group of friends greeted him with friendly salutations:
— Oh, Mr. Ivanitsa, good morning. Did we see them?
— Who?
— The voters. Only peasants, three thousand. We’ve already handed out the ballots to them. Everything is in order. Come now to the school.

They turned down a narrow winding little street and emerged around the polling place. Indeed, a whole mass of townspeople and peasants were humming peacefully and quietly in the yard and the adjoining street. The agitators were moving among them and, half openly, half secretly, handing out ballots to the newly arrived. Here and there, cries could be heard that for whole years they had not shown up for elections.
— Damn it, for the first time in eight years I’m showing up for an election today.
— Me too.
— Me too.
Such confessions were heard from everywhere.

The bureau was already set up in the school hall. Some voters, as well as one of the opposition candidates, were hovering around the bureau. The voting began. Gramatikov found it strange that in the yard next to the school, as well as in the yards on the opposite side of the street, there were crawling numerous heavily armed gendarmes, among whom two bailiffs were moving about and whispering some instructions to them. “But isn’t it forbidden by the electoral law to have an armed force in the vicinity of the polling place! Strange!”

But there was not much room left for surprise... Before Gramatikov’s eyes, there began, whirled, rustled, and roared such a storm of horrors and violence that he stood petrified, as if struck by lightning. Here is what happened: not yet having recovered from the strange impression made on him by the presence of armed force around the polling place, he saw Adamcho Kokoshkarina run up to one of the police officers and, out of breath and flustered, whisper something confusedly into his ear. The officer called a gendarme, said a few words to him, and sent him off. A minute later the district chief appeared. Adamcho whispered something to him. The district chief gave some orders to the officers; they scattered, and before long gendarmes began to emerge from the neighboring houses, leading horses behind them. They mounted the horses, the district chief at their head, with drawn sabre, gave the command “Forward!” and twenty mounted gendarmes, armed to the teeth, rushed down the narrow street clogged with voters, rushed in and began to batter the living wall apart with their horses’ chests. Shouts, cries, uproar, protests, commands, sabres; gleaming in the sun, waves of people surged back and forth, the horses plunged indiscriminately into the crowd, the living wall split to make room for them; new waves from the rear ranks poured in and pushed back the gendarmes with their mass... But force prevailed, and the living wall wavered. The Turkish voters began to vanish one by one: “Не ме лязъм бана даяк еме.” The peasants began to look at one another. The gendarmes managed to push the greater part of the voters back to a considerable distance.

The other, quite small part remained in the schoolyard. Here were Tarnovaliya and Gramatikov. From the opposite side of the street, the shriek of a clarinet began to cut through the air, violins were heard, the noise of an approaching crowd was heard, and a wild thunderclap shattered the surroundings. There they are: the violinists, behind them with lightning in his eyes Bay Ganyo Balkanski, there are Gochoolu and Dochoolu, there is Petrescu, Danka Harsazina’s grandson, Spiro Kopoya, Topal Mustafa, there are the gypsies, the fishermen, there is old Danko Harsazina himself... — Long live the honorable government, hurrah! — shouted Danka’s grandson in a thin voice.
— Hooray... ra... raaaa! — roared the hundred-mouthed, fearsome crowd.
Shivers ran through Gramatikova. The year 1876 flashed through his mind; the bashi-bazouk hordes rose before him again; the name of Fazlŭ Pasha came to his lips.

The wild horde of drunken fiends burst into the schoolyard. Good God! What coarseness, what arrogance, what stupid savagery in those bulging bloodshot eyes, in those swaggering movements, in those provocateur-like glances!... Bay Ganyo, accompanied by his retinue, which roughly made way for him, ascended the stairs and slipped into the school hall, to the desk. There was a noise through the windows, a dull growling, and, pushed by the invading wave, Nikola Tarnovaliya appeared on the stairs. At once Danko’s grandson darted toward him like a bird of prey and, seizing him by the collar, began to tear his throat with a hoarse voice: “Hold him, he’s cursing the prince, he’s insulting the prince, hold him!” Petresku and Danko Harsyzina were not slow to follow. The two of them, like wolves, squeezed him, lifted him up in their arms, and dragged him down the stairs. Bay Ganyo slipped into the hall, took some note from the chairman of the bureau, handed it to Danko’s grandson, who squeezed through the crowd, slipped into the neighboring yard, and after a minute, when the foot and mounted gendarmes burst into the yard, they found Bay Ganyo’s army pinned into a corner by the indignant voters who had remained in the yard. Petresku, with bloodied chest, with hands and face smeared with blood, roared like the most innocent infant. He had already jabbed two or three voters and in time managed to carry out the program—to get bloodied, climb onto a pile of stones, and, at the top of his voice, call for help: “They killed me, Mr. chief, they were going to kill me, I’m shouting ‘Long live the prince,’ and they’re stabbing me with knives!”

The police began their role... “Sabers out!”... The sabers rang, the whips cracked. Protests were heard, but they were drowned out by curses. The police, aided by Bay Ganyo’s army, seized Nikola Tarnovaliya and his more prominent comrades; the mounted gendarmes charged about and swept the yard clean.

And Gramatikov, swept along by the flow of the crowd, found himself in the street. He was as if struck by lightning! In his ears rang the words of Bay Ganyo, who, from the top of the stairs, was shouting: “We too have been more or less in Europe and know these damned things, the elections. I have been in Belgium...”

The words of Grandpa Dobri were ringing in his ears too. Poor Grandpa Dobri! Pushed out into the street, struck hard on the head, with tears in his eyes from illness, from anger, or from pity, he kept speaking up, the poor man, in a broken voice: “Well, Mr. Chief... but didn’t they say... that is, didn’t they say they were supposed to be free... or something like that...” Poor Grandpa Dobri!...
A few days later, Gramatikov read in one of the capital’s newspapers the following telegram:

“Sofia. To the Prime Minister. The elections were conducted in absolute silence and order. Elected: Ganyo Balkanski, Filyo Gochoolu, and Tanas Dochoolu, all of ours. The opposition candidates failed disgracefully. As soon as the voters appeared with music at their head, their gang scattered. The whole city is rejoicing. Long live His Royal Highness. Ganyo Balkanski”

The letter to Gramatikov, which we mentioned above, ended with these words: “And what will the people say, what will they do? A curious question! You used to tell me once that you still believe in the Bulgarian people. Come on then! Don’t mock me! In whom do you believe? In this slave tribe that endures all this? Look at it as portrayed in its representatives.”

The people in whom you believe are slaves, I tell you, slaves; slavery is bliss for them, tyranny is a blessing, servility is heroism, contemptuous snoring from above — music! And yet this people is wretched and unhappy, thrice unhappy! Beaten by fate, condemned to suffer and toil for others, tormented by enemies, and even more by friends and saviors, it had not a single firm point on which to rest its gaze, a handle to lean on; it has lost faith in itself and in its destiny and has become so “practical” and sober, sober to the point of insensibility. Without help, without counsel, crushed and torn apart outwardly and inwardly, there it is, a sad remnant of old times, scattered by storms...
Is there anyone who can revive it, to draw it along after him? — Ideals? — Vanity, wind!...
